source.title: A UGMENT YOUR BATCH : BETTER TRAINING WITH LARGER BATCHES
source.authors: Elad Hoffer; Tal Ben-Nun; Itay Hubara; Niv Giladi; T. Hoefler; Daniel Soudry

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing effective batch size and training recipe changes held-out performance, using batch augmentation and standard large-batch training rather than the original versions’ exact interventions.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own batch-augmentation and regime-adaptation comparisons, reported validation/test metrics, and gradient-correlation measurements related to the batch-size account. Cited prior-work results and throughput-only measurements are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5's recipe-dependent qualification: enlarging effective batches through repeated augmentations improves held-out performance at unchanged epoch budgets. It also reports ordinary larger-batch training with proportionally longer training. It does not directly establish the fixed-epoch penalty from increasing the number of distinct examples per batch.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that composing larger batches from multiple transformed instances improves held-out performance and convergence per epoch while enabling parallel scaling. They present gradient-variance analysis as an explanation and argue that this batch composition can make larger effective batches advantageous.
record.recipe_differences: Uses repeated, differently augmented instances of samples in each batch, changing the effective batch while retaining the original learning-rate schedule and epoch count in the main comparisons; some separate experiments adapt the schedule.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch-augmentation factor M, augmentation type and dataset/model; reported gains vary in magnitude across settings. The paper also reports improved accuracy with a shorter adapted schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmented-image gradient correlations decrease during training and generally exceed correlations between separate images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different augmentations of an image produce correlated gradients, with correlations depending on training state.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch augmentation changes gradient L2 norms during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch augmentation reduces gradient norms relative to baseline, while retaining larger norms than ordinary larger-batch training.

record.problems: The main tables report validation accuracy rather than test error for image classification. Most comparisons do not report uncertainty estimates. Several figure-based results provide no exact values. The shorter-training ResNet44 result changes both learning rate and schedule.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited results about other large-batch methods are excluded because they are prior-work results, not this study's own findings. Throughput measurements are not held-out performance outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.

The fixed-epoch penalty from increasing distinct examples per batch, its workload-dependent threshold, and an ordinary large-batch language-model comparison. Batch augmentation retains distinct examples and updates per epoch while increasing transformed instances and computation.
Adding or removing dropout, dropout strength, and interactions with training-set size or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Table 4's ordinary larger-batch RA outcomes: ResNet44 93.07% versus 93.07% baseline; Wide-ResNet28 + cutout 96.6% versus 96.6%; AlexNet 57.6% versus 58.25%; ResNet50 75.7% versus 76.3%. These are relevant own-study comparator results, not merely method rankings.

Matched-exposure BA results missing from the rows: ResNet44 M=10 reaches 93.48%; ResNet44 + cutout M=10 reaches 94.3%; Wide-ResNet28 + cutout M=10 reaches 96.95%. These distinguish BA from simply exposing the model to more augmented instances.

ImageNet ResNet50 with BA and adjusted schedules reaches 76.86% at 40 epochs and 75.7% at 23 epochs, versus the baseline's 76.3% at 90 epochs. Record these separately from unchanged-schedule and distributed comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the listed versions. Its main results support V5's recipe-dependent qualification, not the ordinary fixed-epoch large-batch penalty. Smaller accuracy gains are not scope limitations when the tested proposition is avoiding that penalty. Image outcomes are called validation accuracy by the paper, and most lack uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out accuracy on natural labels are not measured.
No width sweep past interpolation is reported.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures is reported.

The study varies effective batch size through batch augmentation, but does not test ordinary large batches against small batches with a fixed epoch budget as the version describes. It does not evaluate the language-model result as a large-batch penalty comparison.
Dropout is used to create distinct intermediate-layer instances in language modeling; the paper does not test adding dropout as the intervention or its standalone effect.
Gradient correlations and gradient norms are measured, but magnitude-aware sharpness is not.
No memorized-example removal experiment is reported.

rows.subject: Word-level LSTM
rows.operation_detail: Batch augmentation with M=10 instances using different Dropout masks; no fine-tuning.
rows.note: Authors characterize the positive effect as more modest than in previous experiments.
rows.check: Change partial to observed for the tested no-penalty qualification: perplexity improves from 58.8 to 58.6. This compares repeated dropout instances, not larger batches of distinct sequences; it does not test V6.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Distributed batch augmentation M=4; B=256 distinct samples, Ghost Batch Normalization of 32 images, standard shorter regime.
rows.note: The text says higher batch augmentation consistently produces increased validation accuracy compared with M=1 baseline.
rows.check: Figure 5 establishes M=4 as the comparator for M=10. The supplied discussion does not establish its held-out improvement over M=1; the listed M=1 numbers concern throughput.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Distributed batch augmentation M=10; B=256 distinct samples, Ghost Batch Normalization of 32 images, standard shorter regime.
rows.note: The text says higher batch augmentation consistently produces increased validation accuracy compared with M=1 baseline.
rows.check: Correct the comparison to M=10 versus M=4, both at 40 epochs and B=256 distinct samples. The text explicitly reports lower validation error for M=10; it does not establish this comparison against M=1.

rows.subject: ResNet44 + cutout
rows.operation_detail: Regime adaptation with B=640 and 10x more epochs to match instances seen during training.
rows.note: Comparison is against baseline and BA; RA is a comparator, not the tested batch-augmentation intervention.
rows.check: Correct baseline to 93.7% for ResNet44 + cutout; RA reaches 93.8%. This is a valid longer-training result bearing on V5, despite being a comparator. The 93.07% baseline belongs to ResNet44 without cutout.

rows.subject: ResNet44 + cutout
rows.operation_detail: Batch augmentation M=10, larger learning rate, and faster learning-rate decay schedule for shortened training.
rows.baseline: 93.07% with over four times the number of iterations (100 epochs)
rows.note: Combined changes include the learning rate and schedule; not an isolated batch-size comparison.
rows.check: The combined recipe is relevant to V5's adaptation qualification. Preserve the reported 94.15% at 23 epochs, but flag that the text inconsistently describes half the iterations and over four times fewer iterations. Its 93.07% comparator also differs from Table 3's 93.7% cutout baseline.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet classifiers using batch augmentation at unchanged epoch budgets and learning rates
relationships.reason: R1–R12 all exceed baseline held-out accuracy with larger effective batches, supporting V5's adapted-recipe qualification; modest gains in R8, R11 and R12 still avoid a penalty.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest larger augmented batches improved held-out image-classification accuracy without increasing epochs.

relationships.condition: PTB LSTM with repeated sequences receiving different dropout masks
relationships.reason: R13 increases effective batch size from 20 to 200 while test perplexity improves from 58.8 to 58.6, extending the adapted-composition qualification to language modeling.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest repeated sequences with different dropout masks improved perplexity while increasing effective batch size.

relationships.condition: Distributed ImageNet ResNet50 with Ghost Batch Normalization and 40 epochs
relationships.reason: R15 explicitly reports lower validation error for M=10 than the M=4 comparator in R14, supporting successful scaling under this recipe.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest greater instance repetition reduced validation error under the distributed training recipe.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 models with ordinary larger batches and proportionally longer training
relationships.reason: Corrected R16 reaches 93.8% versus 93.7%; missing Table 4 rows show ResNet44 and Wide-ResNet matching their 93.07% and 96.6% baselines, supporting the longer-training qualification.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest proportionally longer training matched or slightly exceeded small-batch CIFAR-10 accuracy.

relationships.condition: ImageNet AlexNet and ResNet50 with larger distinct-example batches and proportionally longer training
relationships.reason: Based on missing Table 4 rows: RA reaches 57.6% versus 58.25% for AlexNet and 75.7% versus 76.3% for ResNet50, showing that this particular longer-training recipe does not fully recover baseline accuracy.
relationships.display_finding: Proportionally longer training reportedly left accuracy below baseline for both architectures, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 ResNet44 with batch augmentation and a shortened, adjusted learning-rate schedule
relationships.reason: R17 reports 94.15% at 23 epochs, supporting successful recipe adaptation, although its comparator and iteration descriptions require correction.
relationships.display_finding: The reported accuracy gain with a shortened adjusted schedule remains unverified, with its comparator and iteration descriptions unresolved.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
